readerTitle: Why Febreze failed until it found a moment to belong to
caseNote: 실제 기업 (P&G Febreze, Duhigg의 서술) + 실제 연구 (Wood 2002, Lally 2010) + 가상 적용 (창문 청소, 회계 사무소)
insight: 습관은 고객의 의지가 아니라 신호에서 나온다. 고객에게 기억하라고 하지 말고, 이미 하는 일 바로 뒤에 제품을 붙여라.
misconception: 좋은 제품이고 고객이 마음에 들어 하면 알아서 꾸준히 쓰게 된다.

sources.text: Duhigg, C. (2012). The Power of Habit. Random House. (Febreze chapter)
Duhigg, C. (2012, Feb 16). How Companies Learn Your Secrets. The New York Times Magazine.
Wood, W., Quinn, J. M., & Kashy, D. A. (2002). Habits in everyday life: Thought, emotion, and action. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(6), 1281–1297.
Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009.

factChecks.note: Febreze 이야기는 Duhigg의 저널리즘 서술에 기반합니다. 테스트 시장 시기(1990년대 중반), 냄새에 둔감해진 고객, 청소 후 뿌리던 여성, 향을 늘려 '청소의 마무리'로 재출시한 흐름을 확인하세요. 구체적 매출 수치는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다. 이야기가 단순화되었을 수 있어 카드에 'as Duhigg tells it'으로 표시했습니다.
'Febreze가 P&G의 가장 큰 브랜드 중 하나로 성장했다'는 표현: 연매출 10억 달러 이상 브랜드로 보도된 자료를 게시 전 확인하세요.
Wood et al.(2002) 일기 연구: 행동의 약 43%가 거의 매일, 대개 같은 장소에서, 다른 생각을 하면서 일어났다는 수치를 원문으로 확인하세요.
Lally et al.(2010): 참가자 96명, 자동화까지 중앙값 66일, 범위 18~254일, 하루 빠뜨려도 형성에 큰 영향 없음. 원문 확인 필요.
창문 청소 업체와 회계 사무소 사례는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The spray that worked, and still didn't sell
body: In the mid-1990s, Procter & Gamble developed a spray that removed bad smells from fabric instead of covering them up. In tests, it worked.
Then it went on sale in a few test cities. Sales were poor. The product did its job. Customers just didn't keep using it.

image.label: A spray bottle forgotten at the back of a cupboard
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 싱크대 아래 수납장 안쪽, 세제 병들 사이에 거의 꽉 찬 무지 스프레이 병 하나가 먼지를 뒤집어쓰고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 라벨은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're on the team. What do you try first?
body: The spray removes odors. Customers who tried it said they liked it. But few bought a second bottle.
You have budget for one move before the next test.

options.text: Run ads showing how embarrassing a smelly home can be
options.feedback: Ads can raise awareness, but they assume people notice the smell in their own home. If they don't, the message lands on someone else.

options.text: Cut the price so buying a second bottle feels easy
options.feedback: A lower price removes one barrier to buying again. It doesn't give anyone a reason to reach for the bottle on a normal Tuesday.

options.text: Watch how people actually clean at home before changing anything
options.feedback: It costs time, but it shows when and why people use the product. That's exactly what P&G's researchers did, and it changed the launch.

cards.title: The people who needed it couldn't smell the problem.
body: As journalist Charles Duhigg tells it in *The Power of Habit*, researchers visited homes. People living with pets or smoke had stopped noticing the smell. Nothing reminded them to spray.
Then they met a woman who sprayed after she finished cleaning a room. Not to fix a smell, but as a small finishing touch.
P&G added more scent and relaunched it as the last step of cleaning. Sales took off, and Febreze grew into one of the company's biggest brands.

cards.title: Habits
body: A **habit** is a behavior that a cue sets off almost automatically. The cue can be a time, a place, or the action you just finished. A routine follows, and a reward makes the loop more likely next time.
The first Febreze had no cue. If you can't smell the problem, nothing prompts you. The relaunch gave it one: a room you just cleaned.
The lesson: don't ask customers to remember you. **Attach to something they already do.**

image.label: Habit loop: cue, routine, reward
image.brief: 원형 화살표 3단계 인포그래픽. "Cue: room just cleaned" → "Routine: spray" → "Reward: fresh smell, job done". 화살표가 다시 처음으로 돌아오는 순환 구조. 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Habits follow the setting, not good intentions.
body: Psychologist Wendy Wood and colleagues asked students to log what they did through the day. About 43% of their actions happened almost daily, usually in the same setting, often while they were thinking about something else.
That is why liking a product predicts repeat use poorly. Customers who intend to use you still forget. The situation they're in decides much more than their plans do.

cards.title: Same work, different cue.
body: A window cleaner has two kinds of customers. Some call "when the windows look dirty." Dirt builds slowly, so they rarely notice, and bookings come at random.
Others are booked for the same week each season, confirmed before the cleaner leaves. They keep coming back. The work is identical. The second group simply has a cue.

image.label: Two calendars: scattered bookings vs regular ones
image.brief: 달력 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽 "Call when dirty"는 예약 표시가 불규칙하게 흩어져 있고, 오른쪽 "Booked each season"은 매 분기 같은 주에 깔끔하게 표시됨. 창문 청소 도구 아이콘.

cards.softwareNote: Apps that stick usually hang off an existing cue: a summary that arrives with the morning email, a dashboard opened in the Monday team meeting. Asking users to "remember to log in" rarely works.

cards.title: Habits form slowly and break when life changes.
body: In a study of 96 volunteers building a new daily habit, it took a median of 66 days to feel automatic, with a range from 18 to 254. Expect a long ramp, not a quick win.

Habits also break when the setting changes: a move, a new job, a new office. That's when customers choose again. It's a risk for you, and an opening against rivals whose customers are in the middle of change.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You do monthly books for small companies. Clients are meant to send their receipts each month. Many forget, so you chase them and close the books late.
Which change is most likely to make sending receipts a habit?

options.text: Send firmer monthly reminders that warn about late filing
options.feedback: Reminders create a cue, but an outside one that's easy to ignore. You'd still be the one doing the remembering.

options.text: Give each client an address to forward receipts to the moment they arrive
options.feedback: It hooks onto something clients already do: opening the email with a receipt. Setup takes effort, but the cue then repeats on its own.

options.text: Offer a small discount to clients who send everything on time
options.feedback: A reward without a cue mostly pays the clients who were already on time. The forgetful ones still forget.

cards.title: Don't ask customers to remember you. Give them a cue.
body: Repeat business rarely comes from motivation. It comes from a reliable moment that comes right before using you.
**Try it today:** write down what a typical customer is doing in the minute before they use your product or service. Is that moment regular enough to build on?
